331.quote_or_event: “As you must, of necessity, one day part with everything, in this transient world of living beings, why do you cling to kingly power?”
331.explanation: The monk Gardabhāli confronts King Sañjaya with the folly of clinging to power and possessions in a world where everything must be given up.
331.tie_back: Valluvar calls it the lowest folly to take the impermanent for the permanent; the monk asks why the king clings to what he must inevitably lose.
331._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit on clinging to the transient, though the Kural frames the error as false cognition rather than attachment.

332.quote_or_event: “Then at one time, his manifold savings are a large treasure. Then at another time, his heirs divide it, or those who are without a living steal it, or the king takes it away, or it is ruined in some way or other, or it is consumed by the conflagration of the house.”
332.explanation: The Ācārāṅga describes wealth that accumulates into a great treasure and then scatters through heirs, thieves, the king, ruin or fire.
332.tie_back: The Kural likens wealth to a crowd that gathers for a show and disperses when it ends; the Ācārāṅga traces the same gathering and dispersal of riches.
332.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
332._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close match on the coming and going of wealth, without the Kural's theatre simile.

333.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
333.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī tells King Ishukāra that riches are left behind at death and only dharma endures.
333.tie_back: The Kural urges using unstable wealth at once for lasting deeds; the Uttarādhyayana likewise contrasts possessions that must be left with the Law that alone endures.
333._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; partial fit: it shares the contrast between perishable wealth and enduring dharma, but the queen urges renunciation rather than spending wealth on good deeds.

334.quote_or_event: “Mankind is harassed by Death; it is taken hold of by Old Age; the days are called unfailing… The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
334.explanation: Bhṛgu's sons explain that the days pass unfailingly while death and old age seize humanity, and each lost day is gone for ever.
334.tie_back: Valluvar unmasks the ordinary day as a saw cutting away life; the Jain verses likewise reveal each passing day as irrecoverable life lost.
334._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi notes 'days' is literally 'nights'); a close thematic match without the saw image.

335.quote_or_event: “He who can call Death his friend, or who can escape him, or who knows that he will not die, might perhaps decide: this shall be done tomorrow.”
335.explanation: The young men refuse to postpone the religious life, since no one can count on escaping death until tomorrow.
335.tie_back: The Kural urges doing good before the tongue fails and the death rattle comes; this verse likewise forbids putting off dharma to an uncertain tomorrow.
335._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; near match on urgency in the face of death, lacking the Kural's physical deathbed imagery.

336.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
336.explanation: Mahāvīra tells Gautama that human life ends as suddenly as a withered leaf drops from its tree.
336.tie_back: The Kural's ironic 'greatness' of the world, where one alive yesterday is gone today, matches Mahāvīra's image of lives falling like leaves.
336._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong on the transience of life, but without the Kural's irony and its stress on yesterday versus today.

337.quote_or_event: “I have this, and I have not that; I must do this, and I should not do that! While he talks in this strain, the robbers (viz. time) drag him away. What foolishness is this!”
337.explanation: A man busy reckoning his possessions and plans is carried off by time before he finishes.
337.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who cannot be sure of one moment yet make endless plans; the Jain verse shows the planner dragged away by time mid-sentence.
337._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; very close fit on endless planning cut off by death.

338.quote_or_event: “(The soul) cannot be apprehended by the senses, because it possesses no corporeal form, and since it possesses no corporeal form it is eternal. The fetter of the soul has been ascertained to be caused by its bad qualities, and this fetter is called the cause of worldly existence.”
338.explanation: Answering the materialist claim that the soul is produced by and perishes with the body, Bhṛgu's sons say the soul is formless and eternal, only temporarily bound to embodiment by karma.
338.tie_back: The Kural pictures body and soul as egg (or nest) and bird, the one abandoned when the other leaves; the Jain verse likewise holds the soul to be distinct from the body and only temporarily joined to it.
338._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; doctrinally parallel (soul distinct from body) but lacks the Kural's image of departure and abandonment.

339.quote_or_event: Jain doctrine describes passing from one birth to the next as almost instantaneous: at death the soul, carrying its karmic body, moves to its next embodiment in at most a few moments (vigraha-gati), so death and rebirth follow each other continuously, like falling asleep and waking.
339.explanation: In Jain cosmology there is no long gap between lives; the embodied soul leaves one body and takes the next almost at once until liberation ends the cycle.
339.tie_back: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Jain teaching on transmigration likewise treats death and rebirth as one continuous passage, though it uses no sleep metaphor.
339.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.25–30 (on vigraha-gati, the soul's transit between births)
339._accuracy_note: Next-best match only: paraphrased from general knowledge of Tattvārtha Sūtra ch. 2, not verified live, and the sleep–waking analogy is the Kural's own, not found in the Jain source.

340.quote_or_event: “Going through the same religious practices as perfected saints, you will reach the world of perfection, Gautama, where there is safety and perfect happiness.”
340.explanation: Mahāvīra points Gautama to Siddha-loka, the abode of the perfected at the summit of the universe, the soul's only permanent home.
340.tie_back: The Kural suggests the soul only lodges in the body because it has not yet found a lasting home; Jainism names that home as the world of perfection reached at liberation.
340._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; fits the commentators' reading (true home = liberation), but the verse does not describe the body as a temporary lodging.
